question: A leaked report (ref. 12595/2023)1 drawn up by Frontex’s Fundamental Rights Office places blame on the Greek authorities.

Specifically, the report states that: - the Greek authorities failed to initiate a search and rescue operation as they should have done after receiving the Frontex alert; - attempts by the Greek coastguard to tow the Adriana put the 700 or so passengers on board the vessel at even greater risk; - the Greek coastguard vessel PPLS 920 recorded the Adriana lurching in a dangerous manner; - attaching ropes to the boat posed significant risks; - contrary to the claims made by the Greek authorities, the Adriana had been sailing without a working engine for quite some hours; - the resources deployed by the Greek authorities were insufficient; - the immediate focus of the Greek authorities prior to the shipwreck was not on carrying out a search and rescue; - the Greek authorities delayed starting a search and rescue operation and only initiated one when the Adriana capsized, by which time it was too late to rescue all passengers; - the Greek authorities did not make use of the resources offered to them by Frontex.
In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does the conduct of the Greek authorities, as outlined above, comply with the legal obligation2to rescue persons in peril and with EU rules on search and rescue?
Knowing all of the above, was it not Frontex’s duty to intervene in the context of its mandate?
answer: 1. The Commission is aware of the findings of the Serious Incident Report that was drawn up by the Frontex Fundamental Rights Officer. Actors involved in search and rescue (SAR) operations must act in a lawful, swift and coordinated way to make sure that those in distress at sea are brought to safety as rapidly as possible independently from the circumstances.

The Commission is in regular contact with Greece, continues to call for the national investigations and judicial proceedings to be conducted in a prompt and comprehensive manner and expects the authorities to prosecute any wrongdoing, as is their responsibility. 2. The duty to render assistance to persons in distress at sea is a legal obligation for Member States under international law (3).

The Commission has no legal competence to conduct SAR operations or to designate placed for disembarkations. National rescue coordination centres retain the sole responsibility to launch or coordinate SAR operations.

As per the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation (4), Frontex is obliged to make its assets available and provide technical and operational assistance in support of SAR operations that may arise in the context of border surveillance operations at sea.

In its Decision of 26 February 2024 (5), the European Ombudsman noted that in this case, Frontex has not breached any relevant rules concerning its emergency response obligations, although the report identified areas for improvement to help prevent tragedies in future.

As part of the comprehensive approach to SAR set out in the New Pact on Asylum and Migratio n (6), the Commission and relevant EU Agencies will continue — within the remits of their competence — to support Member States in improving their cooperation in relation to SAR.

Under the United Nations Geneva Convention of 1951, in particular Article 33 thereof, the Protocol of 1967 relating to the Status of Refugees, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea of 1982 (Unclos), the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea of 1974 (SOLAS) and the International Convention on Maritime Search and Rescue (SAR) of 1979. https://home-affairs.ec.europa.
